title: Network Cables
description: Copper, fiber, and which wire goes where
tagline: Copper, fiber, and which wire goes where

sections.title: Copper — Twisted Pair (UTP)
sections.body: The most common cable in offices: 8 thin copper wires twisted into 4 pairs (twisting reduces interference), ending in an RJ-45 plug that clicks into your switch like a phone charger.

sections.title: Straight-Through vs Crossover
sections.body: Two ways to wire the RJ-45 ends. The old rule is simple:
sections.code:
T568B order (straight-through, both ends):
1 Orange-W  2 Orange   3 Green-W  4 Blue
5 Blue-W    6 Green    7 Brown-W  8 Brown

sections.title: Fiber Optic — Light Speed
sections.body: Fiber sends light through glass instead of electricity through copper. It ignores electrical noise completely and travels MUCH farther — that is why ISPs and data centers love it.
points: Single-mode (yellow): tens of kilometers, used by providers.
Downside: costs more and is trickier to install than copper.

sections.title: The Console Cable
sections.body: A special cable from your laptop to a device console port. It carries no network traffic — it just gives you a command-line window so you can configure a brand-new switch/router (exactly what our CLI labs simulate).

sections.title: 30-Second Cheat Sheet
points: UTP copper → up to 100 m → cheap default choice.
Fiber → long distance + zero interference → higher cost.
Straight-through → unlike devices. Crossover → like devices.
sections.tip: 💡 Modern ports have Auto-MDIX which fixes a wrong cable automatically — but CCNA still tests the classic straight vs crossover rule!
